problem: Visuomotor navigation policies (GNM, ViNT, OmniVLA) imitate teleoperated demonstrations that contain operator noise and bias, so they inherit safe-but-suboptimal behavior and often approach obstacles too closely or ignore dynamic agents. Datasets provide only one executed trajectory per observation and no supervision over alternative feasible actions.
motivation: Humans implicitly compare multiple possible trajectories in a scene and choose those that lower risk, but this counterfactual reasoning is absent from policy training. Human preference labels over counterfactual trajectories under identical observations could supply a scalable safety-alignment signal without online interaction.
key_idea: Augment a navigation dataset (SCAND) with human pairwise preferences over counterfactual trajectories for each observation, then fine-tune visuomotor policies to imitate the most-preferred trajectory.
insight: Human-preferred counterfactuals often beat the demonstrated trajectory (the dataset trajectory was not preferred in 70.51% of scenes), so distilling them yields safer behavior than pure imitation. Annotators often picked stopping, a behavior nearly absent in SCAND, and CHOP-aligned policies then learned to stop and wait in real-world tight dynamic scenarios. Gains vary by base model: ViNT improves much less, and its baseline is already weak, suggesting preference alignment cannot fix limited base capability. No ablation of the pipeline components (e.g., annotator-target versus perturbation candidates) is reported.
method: Counterfactual trajectory generation: for each observation, M=4 candidates of N=8 waypoints: the dataset trajectory, a human-guided candidate (annotator clicks a target in the image and the trajectory shape is reparameterized to end there, or the annotator picks a stop/zero-motion trajectory), and rotated shape-preserving perturbations (uniform clockwise/counterclockwise) of the dataset trajectory.

Human preference annotation: annotators see the image with two overlaid trajectories and choose the safer/more appropriate one, considering clearance, collision risk and goal reaching. This gives C(4,2)=6 pairwise labels per scene, 1,127,520 in total over 187,920 observations. Eight annotators; target-providers and preference-labelers are disjoint.
Best-trajectory selection: the trajectory with the most pairwise wins is chosen as tau*. Ties are broken by preferring annotator-suggested trajectories, then the dataset trajectory, then random.

Preference-based fine-tuning: an L2 imitation loss ||tau_hat - tau*||^2 to the preferred trajectory (a simple SFT instantiation, no reward model or RL). ViNT and GNM are fine-tuned end-to-end; OmniVLA (7.5B) uses LoRA (rank 32, ~3% trainable weights).

Deployment: a ROS2 asynchronous plan-execute stack. A model runner publishes waypoints, a path manager prunes traversed waypoints and re-frames them into the current odometry, and a waypoint-tracking planner outputs cmd_vel. The stack is model-agnostic.

setting.backbone: OmniVLA (7.5B, LoRA fine-tuned), ViNT (fine-tuned end-to-end), GNM (fine-tuned end-to-end)
setting.model_size: OmniVLA 7.5B; ViNT and GNM smaller (size not stated)
setting.training_data: SCAND augmented with the CHOP preference set: 187,920 annotated observations, 4 counterfactuals each, 1.13M pairwise labels. 124 ROS bags, 20% (25) held out for testing, the rest for train/val. Pretrained checkpoints are fine-tuned.
setting.observation: egocentric monocular RGB (with temporal context of 5 frames for ViNT/GNM) plus a goal (goal image / sampled goal position); no depth or LiDAR at inference
setting.action_space: short-horizon predicted waypoint trajectory (8 waypoints for OmniVLA, 5 for ViNT/GNM), tracked by a waypoint controller issuing velocity commands
setting.simulator: real world only (offline SCAND replay plus real robot)
setting.privileged: none at inference. LiDAR is used only for evaluation metrics, and human annotations only in training.

numbers.eval_set_note: held-out 20% of bags (25 recordings) of SCAND test split, per-frame offline evaluation
numbers.extra: fine-tuned on CHOP preference labels; metrics vs base OmniVLA 2453 / 0.6345 / 2.7647

numbers_note: Real-world results are given per scenario for each model (only some rows are listed; ViNT + CHOP and GNM Scenario 2 are omitted for brevity: GNM + CHOP Scenario 2 SR 0.0, clearance 1.07, collisions 1.25, PC 0.463; ViNT + CHOP SR 0.0/0.0/20.0). No standard VLN/ObjectNav benchmarks. The number of runs per scenario is not stated explicitly (success percentages imply 5).
results: Across the three models, CHOP fine-tuning reduces offline near-collisions by 25.9-63.4% (49.7% on average), reduces deviation from preferred trajectories, and raises clearance (+9.7 to +38.1%). On the Vision60 quadruped, OmniVLA and GNM gain in success rate and path completion (e.g. OmniVLA Scenario 3: 0% to 100% SR), while ViNT is inconsistent (SR 40 to 20 in Scenario 3). The average real-world gains are +24.4% goal success and -45.7% collisions/interventions, compared against the pretrained base models.
limitations: Only a simple best-trajectory SFT instantiation is tested; reward modeling and pairwise ranking are left for future work, and there is no ablation of candidate types or of the preference signal versus pure imitation.
Small real-world evaluation (three scenarios, few runs per cell) with inconsistent results for ViNT, and some cells worse after CHOP (e.g. ViNT collisions, clearance in Scenario 3).
Offline metrics use LiDAR-derived proxies and deviation from CHOP-preferred trajectories, which is partly circular with the training target; the dataset is built only on SCAND.
